video_title: The Coolest Year for the Rest of Our Lives? with Zeke Hausfather | TGS 236
gist: Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather forecasts that a record super El Niño will push 2027 to about 1.8C above pre-industrial, and explains why aerosol cuts, scenario revisions and sensitivity drive the 3C-by-2100 baseline. He also covers AI agent energy use and carbon removal work at Frontier and Stripe.

insights.claim: Zeke Hausfather expects 2026 to be the warmest or second-warmest year on record by only a small margin, but 2027 to be much warmer because global temperature lags El Niño peaks by about three to five months.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Record-heat headlines, and the attention and damages that follow, are concentrated in 2027 rather than this year.

insights.claim: Hausfather's latest estimate is that 2027 will be about 1.8C above pre-industrial, versus a previous record of about 1.5C.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A 0.3C jump over the prior record would be an outsized step that could shift policy and market attention to climate.
insights.quote: my latest estimate is that 2027 will be about 1.8 degrees above pre-industrial levels

insights.claim: Past strong El Niños show the pattern: 1997 was near-record and 1998 beat it by a huge margin, and likewise 2015 then 2016 and 2023 then 2024, so the year after the peak sets the record.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The analog set supports forecasting the record year as the one following the El Niño peak.

insights.claim: Strong El Niños add about 0.2C to annual temperatures the year after they peak, perhaps 0.3C this time, while human emissions add about 0.2C every eight years, so humans add a permanent super El Niño worth of heat every eight years.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A strong El Niño is a preview of the average climate roughly a decade out.
insights.quote: we're essentially adding a permanent super El Niño worth of heat to the climate system every eight years

insights.claim: The current El Niño is above 3C anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region in mid-September, more than a degree above any previous event at this point, and is expected to peak near 4C versus the prior record of about 2.75C (1877-78 and 2015-16).
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The event is outside the historical record, so analog-based forecasts carry added uncertainty.

insights.claim: The 1877-1878 El Niño was associated with droughts and famines that killed an estimated 50 million people, and the current event hits regions like Southern Africa, India, Indonesia, northern Brazil and Australia with drier conditions.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Agricultural output risk in these regions is elevated into 2027.

insights.claim: The record El Niño coincides with fertilizer shortages, Strait of Hormuz disruption and cuts to global aid funding (USAID, some European donors), which compounds food-security risk, especially in Africa.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens and Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Food price and famine risk stack across several shocks; Nate Hagens cited chat-group forecasts of caloric shortages in 2028.

insights.claim: The WMO has run the largest mobilization in its history for this El Niño, and countries such as Kenya (livestock vaccines) and southern African states (food stocks, drought-tolerant seeds) are preparing.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Preparation lowers but does not remove the humanitarian and agricultural impact.

insights.claim: Hausfather says future warming comes down to three uncertainties: what humans do (about half the uncertainty), how the biosphere and carbon cycle respond, and climate sensitivity to feedbacks from water vapor, clouds and albedo.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Narrowing any one factor does not narrow the overall range; scenario choice matters as much as physics.

insights.claim: With emissions flat at today's roughly 40 Gt CO2 a year (about 60 Gt CO2-equivalent), Hausfather expects about 3C by 2100 with a range of roughly 2.2C to 4C, and a policy-rollback world would reach about 3.5C (2.5 to 4.5C).
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The central case is far above Paris targets, and tail risk of 4C argues for planning beyond the median.
insights.quote: In that world, we end up at about three degrees, uh, by 2100

insights.claim: In a high-emissions scenario Hausfather sees a non-trivial, roughly one-in-four chance of about 5C warming by 2150.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Tail outcomes extend well past 2100 since warming continues unless emissions reach zero.

insights.claim: The last IPCC report put equilibrium climate sensitivity at 2C to 5C per CO2 doubling (90 percent range), and high-sensitivity models also need high aerosol cooling, because otherwise they would already show about 2C of warming.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Aerosol and sensitivity uncertainties are correlated, so a high-sensitivity world means more warming as aerosols are cleaned up.

insights.claim: If emissions fall to zero, falling atmospheric CO2 and continued ocean warming roughly cancel, so warming stops but the planet does not cool back down without net CO2 removal or climate engineering.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: There is little warming in the pipeline, but also no natural reversal, which is the structural case for carbon removal.

insights.claim: The new CMIP7 emission scenarios are named high, medium, low and very low, and the high scenario now reflects an SSP3-like world where emissions are only about 50 percent above today by 2100, rather than the earlier RCP8.5 tripling of emissions with five times more coal.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Clean energy economics have removed the extreme coal-heavy tail from mainstream scenarios.

insights.claim: Hausfather argues that even in a poor, conflict-ridden world solar is cheap enough that coal use falls by 2100, meaning cheap clean energy is the main reason high-end emission scenarios have been marked down.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Energy-cost curves, not climate policy, are driving the downgrade of worst-case emission paths.

themes.theme: Energy transition: what the data show

insights.claim: Hausfather says global coal use has plateaued since about 2015, gas has grown sharply, oil has flattened as EVs spread, and fossil use is growing under 1 percent a year versus over 3 percent a few decades ago.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Fossil demand growth is slowing but has not peaked in absolute terms.

insights.claim: About 30 percent of cars sold globally this year are electric versus about 5 percent in the US, and the Middle East situation is raising oil prices and accelerating the shift to alternatives.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The US is a laggard in EV adoption while oil demand is being eroded elsewhere.

insights.claim: Wind and solar are set to generate more electricity than natural gas globally this year for the first time.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A milestone showing renewables overtaking a major fossil source in the power mix.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens counters that from 2015 to 2025 solar grew about 4,400 TWh while coal, gas and oil grew about 14,000 TWh, so cheaper solar has added to total energy rather than displacing fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: The additive-versus-substitution view challenges the idea that falling renewable costs alone reduce emissions.

insights.claim: Hausfather says China is about to have a third year of flat-to-falling CO2 emissions, the US and Europe are down about 20 percent and the UK about 40 percent, and the UK now burns no coal.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Peak-emissions evidence is emerging in the largest economies, though global emissions have not yet declined.

insights.claim: Hausfather claims that about $2.3 trillion globally goes to reducing emissions versus well under 1 percent on carbon removal, and Hagens notes this spending has not yet reduced absolute global emissions, which Hausfather concedes.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Capital allocation to carbon removal is tiny relative to abatement spending.

themes.theme: Aerosols and the acceleration of warming

insights.claim: Hausfather attributes essentially all of the recent acceleration in warming, from roughly 0.2C per decade to closer to 0.3C per decade, to falling aerosol emissions on top of continued greenhouse gas emissions.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Cleaner air is unmasking warming, which is a one-time boost that ends once sulfur reaches zero.
insights.quote: pretty much all of the acceleration we've seen in the rate of warming in recent years

insights.claim: Aerosols are estimated to have cooled the planet by between 0.2C and 1.2C versus pre-industrial, a range so wide that at 1.2C the world would be about 2.5C warmer without them.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Aerosol cooling is a major unquantified term in the climate budget.

insights.claim: Global sulfur dioxide emissions are down 40 percent from the 1980 peak, China cut its emissions 75 percent since 2008, and the 2020 low-sulfur shipping fuel rule cut shipping sulfur by about 80 percent, which matters because ships emit in clean marine air where the cloud effect is larger.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Policy-driven clean-air gains had measurable climate side-effects.

insights.claim: Satellite measurements of Earth's energy imbalance from CERES show it rising, possibly from aerosol cuts but possibly from low-cloud feedbacks; if it is feedbacks, warming keeps accelerating rather than ending when sulfur hits zero.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Whether the energy imbalance reflects aerosols or cloud feedback is the key open question distinguishing benign from worrying outcomes.

insights.claim: Methane accounts for about 0.4C of historical warming but, unlike CO2, breaks down in roughly a decade, so cutting methane emissions could actually cool the planet while cutting CO2 only slows warming.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Methane is the fast lever for near-term cooling.

insights.claim: Recent growth in atmospheric methane appears driven mainly by wetlands, possibly a temperature-mediated feedback in tropical wetlands, with permafrost methane still minor globally.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A natural feedback source of methane would be outside direct policy control.

insights.claim: The ocean has absorbed about 90 percent of the heat trapped by greenhouse gases, with the surface up about 1C, the world 1.4C, land about 2C, and the deep ocean only 0.1-0.2C, which buffers but delays the full effect.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The ocean buffer delays impacts but also means no cooling is available if CO2 falls.

insights.claim: Land-use emissions, mostly deforestation, are about 10 percent of global emissions, around four gigatons of carbon, and stopping warming requires eliminating deforestation as well as cutting fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Forest loss is a separate lever alongside fossil fuel reduction.

themes.theme: AI energy use and AI as an information tool

insights.claim: In 2025 Google reported about 0.24 Wh per typical Gemini prompt and OpenAI about 0.34 Wh per ChatGPT query, but those figures are for non-reasoning chat, whereas reasoning models use about five to ten times more energy.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Headline per-prompt energy figures understate energy use of how AI is actually used today.

insights.claim: Hausfather found a typical Claude Code session used about 0.2 to 1.2 kWh and an average day of agent use 1.2 to 6 kWh, roughly two fridges, based on four months of his own usage data.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Agentic AI use consumes orders of magnitude more electricity per task than single prompts, which matters for data-center demand.
insights.quote: a typical, uh, session of using cloud code, you know, was somewhere between point two and one point two kilowatt hours

insights.claim: Hausfather applies Jevons paradox to compute: as AI gets cheaper and more embedded and autonomous, total energy use will rise, as LED lighting cut costs 10x but lumen use rose about 3x.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains in AI are unlikely to cap aggregate electricity demand.

insights.claim: Hausfather says machine learning has struggled with physics-based climate simulation, though AI weather models are strong, so AI will mostly help climate modelling through faster code, downscaling and cloud parameterization rather than replace models.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: AI is a tool for climate modeling, not a shortcut around physics-based projections.

insights.claim: Hausfather is cautiously optimistic that LLMs act as consensus machines that give similar climate answers regardless of political affiliation, because it is hard to train a model that denies climate but answers physics correctly.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: AI might recenter expertise in a fragmented information environment.

themes.theme: Policy, data infrastructure and carbon removal

insights.claim: US cuts to NOAA data products, climate.gov and the 40-year sea ice satellite record and the withdrawal from the IPCC are being offset by Copernicus rebuilding data aggregation, but gaps in unreplaced satellites can never be filled retroactively.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Observational gaps are the irreversible risk, whereas analysis functions can migrate to other institutions.

insights.claim: Hausfather views climate attention as thermostatic and a political luxury good, so extreme events from El Niño and accelerating warming will bring more attention back to climate after a dip since 2022.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Expect political and capital focus on climate to rise with 2027 extremes.

insights.claim: Hausfather's favored policy lever is putting a price on carbon to internalize social costs, and he sees carbon removal as about 10 percent of the solution, with 90 percent from cutting emissions.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Pricing carbon is the standard economist answer, but the political path is described as unlikely by both speakers.

insights.claim: Frontier and Stripe are using this decade to test carbon removal approaches including enhanced rock weathering on croplands (Brazil, India, US, Africa), river liming (Carbon Run), ocean alkalinity enhancement, biomass-based capture and direct air capture, to have scalable options for the 2040s and 2050s.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Carbon removal is at an R&D stage with agriculture-linked methods showing early promise.
